extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator / educated early-18th-century English public
extracted.subtask_description: Moral and social essays from a periodical (The Spectator) offering normative judgments about character, behaviour, and public manners; includes exemplifying letters and short narratives. Aimed at shaping conduct and taste of a general literate audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of Zeal (genuine vs false)
rubrics_metrics.description: Zeal 'has so many Passions which hide themselves under it' — what a man calls zeal for his religion is often 'either Pride, Interest, or Ill-nature.' Genuine zeal should be scrutinised by examining these motives and the heart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine motives before praising zeal: if it stems from pride, desire for precedence, private interest, or malice, it is false zeal. A test offered: true zeal would be 'much more angry with a Sinner than a Heretick.' Beware of self-deception where 'zeal' is invoked for private vanity or advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zeal judged by its means and effects (anti‑persecution criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Zeal that employs 'Racks and Gibbets, Gallies and Dungeons; when he imprisons Mens Persons, confiscates their Estates, ruins their Families, and burns the Body to save the Soul' is declared criminal and an argument that 'his Faith is vain, and his Religion unprofitable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate religious fervour by whether it resorts to coercion, violence, or persecution. If supposed zeal produces imprisonment, confiscation, torture, or burning, it is not genuine benefit to religion or society and should be condemned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest as a motive masquerading as zeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Interest 'is likewise a great Inflamer' — men may persecute or proselytise under colour of zeal because they 'are glad to gain Numbers on his Side' and thereby strengthen their private opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect proselytising or zeal-driven activity that primarily increases an individual's or faction's power or numbers. Look for behaviour where conversion or advocacy serves the actor's reputation or advantage rather than genuine moral ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ill‑nature/revenge disguised as zeal
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Zeal is therefore a great Ease to a malicious Man, by making him believe he does God Service, whilst he is gratifying the Bent of a perverse revengeful Temper.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When zeal enables personal rancour, malice, or revenge—using religion as cover for settling scores—that zeal is spurious. Watch for vindictive impulses clothed in moral language; they reveal ill-nature rather than piety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Atheist/infidel zeal and bigotry
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist 'Zealots in Atheism' — infidelity is 'propagated with as much Fierceness and Contention, Wrath and Indignation, as if the Safety of Mankind depended upon it.' Atheists can be as bigoted and rancorous as religious zealots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess opponents (including infidels) on the temper of their advocacy: fierceness, contention, and intolerance indicate the same defects found in false religious zeal. Avoid equating disbelief with superior moderation; evaluate behaviour and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious belief evaluated by moral and social consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if some articles of faith were mistaken, adherence to Christianity is defended because 'the great Points of the Christian Religion... produce naturally such Habits of Virtue' and 'contribute to the heightning of Morality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge religious systems in part by their practical effects on virtue, charity, social order, and personal conduct. A belief system that promotes moral habits and improves human conduct has public value regardless of metaphysical debates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of a 'jilt' (identifying an injurious coquette)
rubrics_metrics.description: A jilt differs from a coquet: the coquet seeks admiration, the jilt 'must add... a certain Delight in being a Torment to others.' Signs include sudden indifference after encouraging a lover, affectation that alternates with familiarity, artificial plots, perplexing letters from unknown hands, and pleasure in making lovers uneasy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise behavioural patterns: inconsistent warmth and coldness, deliberate teasing, creating rivalries, and manufacturing intrigues are anti-patterns. Examples given (Kitty, Hyæna, Biblis, Chloe) illustrate how such conduct wastes suitors' time and fortune and should be guarded against.

rubrics_metrics.name: When praise/admiration is meaningful
rubrics_metrics.description: One should 'contemn the Praise of the Ignorant' and prefer being tried 'only by his Peers.' 'The Character of the Person who commends you is to be considered'—praise from the ignorant is mere goodwill, not a true attestation of merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value approbation from virtuous, intelligent, and competent judges rather than popular applause. Use inner conscience and approval of worthy peers as measures of true reputation. Beware the giddiness of crowd praise and seek the attestation of reasonable, discerning minds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pandering dedications and seeking ignorant patronage
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Dedications to ignorant Men are as absurd as any of the Speeches of Bulfinch'—addressing works to patrons who cannot appreciate or judge them is misguided and often amounts to pandering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and men of merit should not flatter or seek reputation from those incapable of appreciating the work. Direct efforts toward audiences or patrons who understand and can properly evaluate the contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper parental behaviour versus cruelty (anti‑pattern shown by letter)
rubrics_metrics.description: The printed father's letter ('You are a sawcy audacious Rascal... I'll break your Head... If you Starve in the Streets, I'll never give any thing...') exemplifies cruel, inconsistent, and violent parental conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the letter as a negative exemplar: threats, incoherent punishments, and unconditional repudiation are unethical parental behaviours. Readers are invited to judge such cruelty as blameworthy and contrary to proper parental duty.
